<reason>Side B built a much stronger, well-integrated case and decisively won the central clash over coerced treatment versus incarceration. Side B established clear mechanisms for why punitive enforcement increases overdoses (isolated use, witness fear of calling 911, and post-jail tolerance loss causing fatal relapse) and downstream crime (criminal records blocking employment and police hours wasted on possession arrests). When Side A tried to evade the post-jail tolerance trap by claiming punitive enforcement relies on continuous clinical care and medical detention rather than jail cells, Side B exposed the contradiction: Side A had stripped out criminal penalties and retreated to civil/medical tools that remain available under decriminalization. Side B also directly answered Side A's pressure question on property crime with medication-assisted treatment and employability, whereas Side A became repetitive in the late rounds and included nonexistent reference IDs ([C2.2, C2.4]).</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's pressure question in [B3.1] and follow-through in [B5.1]-[B5.3], which trapped Side A between claiming treatment requires a "criminal penalty" [A2.2] and claiming its "coercive backstop" is merely graduated outpatient/residential care and medical detention [A4.1] rather than jail.</best_rebuttal>
